cards.title: Word problem for one-relation monoids
cards.formal: Is the uniform word problem for ordinary one-relation monoids decidable? Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine which, given any finite alphabet \(A\) and four finite words \(u,v,s,t\in A^*\), always halts and decides whether \(s\) and \(t\) represent the same element of the monoid \(\langle A\mid u=v\rangle\)? The presentation and the word pair are all parts of the input; no running-time bound is prescribed.
cards.definitions:
The free monoid \(A^*\) consists of all finite literal strings over \(A\), including the empty word \(\varepsilon\), with concatenation as multiplication and \(\varepsilon\) as identity. The monoid \(\langle A\mid u=v\rangle\) is the quotient \(A^*/{\equiv}\), where \(\equiv\) is the least equivalence relation containing \(u\equiv v\) and satisfying \(p\equiv q\Rightarrow xpy\equiv xqy\) for all words \(x,y\). Equivalently, \(s\equiv t\) if and only if some finite sequence \(s=w_0,w_1,\ldots,w_k=t\) exists in which every adjacent pair is \((xuy,xvy)\) or \((xvy,xuy)\) for some \(x,y\in A^*\). A zero-step sequence is allowed.

The four words are fully supplied literal strings, not variables to be instantiated by unknown strings. The two relation sides and the tested words may be empty. Replacing an empty side means inserting the other side at a gap in the current finite word. The relation may have equal sides and may preserve or change length. The alphabet itself may be empty, in which case every word is empty. There are no inverse symbols with automatic cancellation, group axioms, cancellation laws or commutativity laws beyond consequences of the single stated monoid relation.

The input explicitly gives an integer alphabet size \(a\ge0\), identifies \(A\) with \(\{1,\ldots,a\}\), and lists all four words with binary letter indices and lengths. This is finite ordinary string input, with malformed encodings rejectable. One ordinary deterministic program must give exact YES/NO answers for all valid presentations and all pairs, terminating on both answers. It receives no oracle, nonuniform advice, random coins or unbounded precomputed data for a presentation. No numerical approximation arises. This is uniform decidability across presentations; a separate non-effectively chosen algorithm for each fixed presentation has different quantifiers.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof that the displayed language of presentation-and-word-pair instances is decidable by a total computable function, or a proof of its undecidability. A positive proof must formalize finite words, the single-relation contextual congruence, finite encoding and a uniform algorithm whose termination and both correctness directions hold for all allowed empty and nonempty inputs. A negative reduction must stay inside ordinary one-relation monoids and preserve equality in both directions. A single fixed one-relation monoid with undecidable word problem suffices for a negative answer but is stronger than necessary to refute uniform decidability. A semidecision procedure that halts only on equal words, an unproved termination claim, an exponential derivation-length lower bound, or a negative theorem for inverse monoids, submonoid membership or equations with unknowns does not by itself settle the target. No Lean resolution is asserted by this review.
cards.why: A foundational decidability boundary for rewriting: can reachability under one literal reversible string rule already escape every terminating uniform algorithm?

importance.reason: One of the central minimal-presentation decision problems, connecting string rewriting, algebraic normal forms, computability and reductions between monoids, inverse monoids and groups.

progress.text: Magnus solves the one-relator group word problem; later work solves major ordinary-monoid special cases, without providing a general procedure.
Nyberg-Brodda surveys the unresolved problem, reduction methods, special cases and gaps in earlier claimed arguments.
The survey’s corrigendum fixes historical attributions and technical wording, including nontermination versus literal looping of Adian’s procedure.
Nyberg-Brodda gives monadic one-relation monoids with exponential Dehn functions but decidable word problems, separating short derivations from decidability.
Gray–Reilly prove undecidability for certain two-generator one-relator inverse monoids; their introduction explicitly leaves the ordinary-monoid question open.
The published membership results concern existential membership in generated submonoids, rather than equality of two specified words.
The Diophantine preprint proves undecidability of equation solvability with unknown elements in some one-relation monoids, a broader predicate than this card.
The audit preserves the uniform ordinary-monoid target and score 96, fixes complete word notation and encodings, and adds full Lean acceptance and later-result scope checks.

cards.status_note: Gray–Reilly, 5 August 2026, explicitly retain the ordinary one-relation-monoid word problem as open. Their inverse-monoid theorem, the 2025/2026 submonoid-membership results and the August 2026 Diophantine theorem do not decide equality of two supplied words in the card’s ordinary presentation model. The saved card asks for one uniform machine; the source’s per-presentation wording is distinguished. Bounded checks through 16 September found no matching uniform resolution, not an exhaustive proof of openness.

context_blocks.text: This is a minimal string-transformation problem. There is only one reversible replacement rule, and it can be applied inside any surrounding context. Starting with a word, repeated replacements can generate many others. Equality asks whether the target lies in this reachability set. The alphabet symbols themselves have no hidden arithmetic meaning; any complicated computation would have to emerge from overlaps and repeated applications of this one rule.

An equality has a finite certificate: a sequence of contextual applications of the defining relation connecting the two words. Inequality has no analogous certificate supplied by the presentation itself. A long search with no successful derivation does not decide whether one exists, since intermediate words can have unbounded length.

Length-preserving relations, where \(|u|=|v|\), form a decidable special case. The general problem allows length-changing replacements. Termination of an oriented shortening rule is not sufficient by itself: different irreducible words may still represent the same element. The requested algorithm has no efficiency requirement, so a large computable time bound would still be a positive answer.

The surrounding algebra offers major positive results. Magnus proved decidability for one-relator groups in 1932. For ordinary monoids, classical work handles important cases such as a single relation equating a word to the identity, and presentations satisfying appropriate cycle-free conditions. Group algorithms cannot simply be applied to every monoid presentation: adjoining inverses may identify additional words, so equality in a related group can lose information.

The historical source needs its correction. Nyberg-Brodda’s survey traces the string-rewriting background to Thue, while its 2022 corrigendum identifies Novikov’s 1957 question as the earliest explicit formulation known to the author. The correction also replaces an informal claim that Adian’s procedure may loop with the more precise statement that it may fail to terminate. An infinite computation need not repeat a previously seen state.

There is concrete evidence that short relations can require very long equality proofs. Nyberg-Brodda constructs the family \(\langle a,b | baa(ba)^{N}=a\rangle\) for \(N\ge 2\) with at least exponential Dehn function. Here the Dehn function measures the maximum, over equal word pairs of bounded total input length, of the minimum number of relation applications needed to connect them. Nevertheless, the same paper proves that every monoid in this family has decidable word problem.

Gray and Reilly’s August 2026 paper proves the existence of a two-generator one-relator inverse monoid with undecidable word problem. Inverse monoid presentations are interpreted in a different algebraic theory that includes a generalized inverse operation and its identities. One displayed relation in that theory is not one ordinary string relation in the present sense. The paper’s introduction explicitly retains the ordinary-monoid problem and the relevant reduced-relator inverse-monoid case as open.

Foniqi–Gray–Nyberg-Brodda prove undecidability of submonoid membership for families of one-relation monoids, in a paper published online in 2025 and in the 2026 journal volume. Submonoid membership asks whether an element equals some product of members of a supplied finite generating list. That existential product choice is absent when comparing just two supplied words.

The August 2026 Diophantine result proves undecidability of solving systems of equations with unknown monoid elements and fixed coefficients in certain one-relation monoids. The word problem is a special case of that broader task, so the broader negative theorem does not imply undecidability of the special case on this card. This also distinguishes equality modulo one literal relation from ordinary word equations over a free monoid.

The current card retains its saved uniform target: the presentation varies with the input to one machine. The sources often phrase the general question as decidability for every fixed one-relation monoid. An affirmative uniform theorem would imply all those individual conclusions; a uniform negative theorem need not exhibit a single fixed undecidable monoid. The August 2026 inverse-monoid paper explicitly leaves the ordinary-monoid question open, and the bounded subsequent search found no matching uniform resolution.

sentences: An ordinary one-relation monoid identifies words using one fixed reversible literal replacement rule in arbitrary surrounding contexts.
The question asks whether a single algorithm can decide equality of any two words when the alphabet and defining relation are also supplied.
Empty words and length-changing relations are allowed, and the algorithm must halt on unequal pairs as well as equal ones.
Recent undecidability results for inverse monoids, submonoid membership and equations with unknowns concern different or broader problems.
A resolution would locate a central decidability boundary for equality under minimal finite algebraic presentations.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
